title: How Far Can You Push Six MacBook Airs?
summary: Six spare MacBook Airs with 16 GB each were running a 30B language model between them. I kept loading bigger models to see where they would stop: a 122B model that fills their memory, the same model on one Air alone, and then a 229B and a 397B model that do not fit in their memory at all.
body_markdown:
## Where the first post stopped


[The first post](https://quickchat.ai/post/six-macbook-airs-private-llm-before-lunch) ended with six spare MacBook Airs on a desk, joined in a line by five Thunderbolt cables and running one language model between them. Each has an M2 chip and 16 GB of memory. The model had 30 billion parameters and wrote about 20 tokens a second, a token being roughly a word.


I finished that post with a guess that models of up to about 80 billion parameters would fit. I wanted to know how far the six could really be pushed, so I kept loading bigger models until something stopped me.


## 122 billion


The guess was too low. macOS lets a Mac’s GPU use about three quarters of its memory, and I raised that to 13 GB out of 16. I also stopped[EXO](https://github.com/exo-explore/exo) , the tool that splits the model across the Macs, from loading the part of a model that looks at images. That freed almost another gigabyte on each Mac.


After that Qwen3.5-122B fit. It has **122 billion parameters** and takes 65 GB, about 11 GB on each Mac. It wrote about 10 tokens a second, and **12** after some tuning.


Nothing much bigger would go in. The six GPUs can use about 84 GB between them, and a model needs working space on top of its own size.


## How it runs


For one person asking short questions, the 122B model runs well. The first word comes after about a second, and the rest follows at 12 tokens a second.


It does less well with several people. Four people asking at once got about 17 tokens a second between them, a little over 4 each. EXO sends everyone’s next word through the six Macs as one batch, and each extra person in the batch makes every Mac read more of the model.


## Long documents


Long documents went worse. The first prompt of a few thousand tokens, which is a few pages of text, crashed the cluster. One Mac ran out of memory, and the other five reported that they had lost a peer.


There turned out to be four separate causes, and one of my fixes made the next problem four times worse.


After four changes to EXO the cluster read a prompt of about **57,000 tokens** and found the three facts I had hidden in it, though it took seven minutes before the answer began. At about 73,000 tokens it still crashes.


## Going higher


With a 122B model running, I was curious whether the six could go higher. For that, part of a bigger model would have to live somewhere other than memory.


Qwen3.5-122B is a mixture-of-experts model. Each of its layers contains 256 small specialist networks, called experts, and a word passing through a layer uses only **8 of them** . The experts are almost the whole model, so at any moment most of it sits in memory unused.


Every Mac also has an SSD that reads about 3 GB a second and had nothing to do once the model was loaded. I changed EXO so that each Mac keeps in memory only the experts it has used recently, and reads the others from its SSD when a word asks for them. It took about 200 lines of code. In a test on one layer, the results matched the normal way bit for bit.


## Taking Macs away


The first test did not need a bigger model. I ran the same 122B model on fewer Macs, so that each one was given more than its memory could hold.


On four Macs it wrote 6.5 tokens a second, about half of what six manage. On three it wrote 4.7 and on two 3.2, and each time it still listed the first 40 prime numbers correctly.


With four Macs, each could keep only about two thirds of its experts in memory. It still found the expert it wanted there about nine times out of ten, because consecutive words keep using the same experts.


## One MacBook Air


Then I gave the whole model to a single Air. The first attempt ran out of memory, and the second worked with less memory set aside for experts.


One 16 GB MacBook Air ran a 65 GB model at **1.9 tokens a second** , and it got the primes right. My test still asked for a haiku about six laptops joined in a line by cables, although only one laptop was answering:


> Six screens glow in row,
> Black cables weave them together,
> One network breathes deep.


In that run the Air read about 900 GB from its SSD, nearly twice what the whole disk holds. That does the disk no harm, since it is writing that wears an SSD out.


## 229 billion


The next model up was MiniMax-M2.7, with **229 billion parameters** . It takes 100 GB, more than the 96 GB of memory in all six Macs put together.


The download gave more trouble than the model. It stopped receiving data without reporting any error, and the progress bar stood still for about five hours before I measured how many bytes were actually arriving. After a restart the rest came in twenty minutes. For the next download I wrote a small script that restarts it if nothing arrives for two minutes.


On all six Macs the 229B model wrote **4.9 tokens a second** and answered my test questions correctly.


## 397 billion


Then came Qwen3.5-397B, with **397 billion parameters** .[The copy I used](https://huggingface.co/spicyneuron/Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-MLX-2.6bit) is compressed harder than usual, to about 2.6 bits for each of the model’s numbers, and takes 130 GB. Its author says it answers as well as the usual 4-bit copy, and I did not check that.


To make room I had to delete an older model from every Mac, because each Mac stores the whole model on its disk even though it runs only a sixth of it.


The model answered from all six Macs at **3.4 tokens a second** . It listed the first 40 primes correctly, found three numbers I had hidden in a prompt of about 4,000 tokens, and wrote a haiku:


> Six laptops in line,
> Cables link them side by side,
> Data flows as one.


The model that wrote it is about one and a half times as big as the memory the six GPUs can use.


*Blue fits in memory. Amber reads part of the model from each Mac’s SSD.*


## What stopped it


At 3.4 tokens a second the disks looked like the limit. The first two Macs in the line found their experts in memory only about half the time. I moved some layers from those two Macs to the last two, which raised that to about three quarters, and the speed did not change at all.


Most of each Mac’s time now goes on the parts of the model that always stay in memory, and a MacBook Air can only read its memory so fast. I stopped at 397 billion. The usual 4-bit copy of the same model takes 224 GB, and I would expect it to write one or two tokens a second. The models beyond that take 600 GB or more, and each Air has a 500 GB disk that has to hold the whole model.


## What you can do with it


Six 16 GB Macs hold about 70 GB of model in memory, which means a model of about 120 billion parameters. That is where they run best, at 12 tokens a second for one person with answers that begin after about a second.


A mixture-of-experts model can be bigger than the memory of your Macs if the software reads experts from disk. The released EXO does not do that, so it needs changes like mine. Expect about half the speed once a third of the experts are on disk, and 3 to 10 seconds before the first word.


Plan for one person at a time and for short prompts. Four people asking together share about one and a half times the output of one, and a long document means minutes of waiting.


Each bigger model was slower than the last, and I did not check whether its answers were any better.

## Frequently asked questions


### How big a model can six 16 GB MacBook Airs run?


In memory, about 70 GB of model fits, which was enough for Qwen3.5-122B at 12 tokens a second. With parts of the model read from each Mac’s SSD, the same six ran MiniMax-M2.7 (229B, 100 GB) at 4.9 tokens a second and a 2.6-bit copy of Qwen3.5-397B (130 GB) at 3.4 tokens a second.


### Can a model bigger than your RAM run on a Mac?


Yes, if it is a mixture-of-experts model and the software can read experts from disk as they are needed. Each word uses only a few experts per layer (8 of 256 in Qwen3.5-122B), so a Mac can keep the recently used ones in memory and read the rest from its SSD. This needed changes to EXO that are not in the released version.


### Can one 16 GB MacBook Air run a 100B+ model?


Yes, slowly. One MacBook Air M2 with 16 GB ran Qwen3.5-122B, a 65 GB model, at 1.9 tokens a second, and it still listed the first 40 primes correctly. It kept part of the model in memory and read the rest from its SSD, about 900 GB of reading in one run. Reading does not wear an SSD out.


### How many people can use a six-MacBook LLM cluster at once?


Several can, but they share the speed. On six MacBook Air M2s running Qwen3.5-122B, one person got 12 tokens a second and four people asking together got about 17 between them, a little over 4 each. Every token passes through all six Macs in turn, and each extra person makes every Mac read more of the model.
